  • GyroSplat: A Linear Representation of Fusion Plasma Turbulence with Direct and Differentiable Physics

    Gerald Gutenbrunner, Gianluca Galletti, Andreas Radler, Fabian Paischer, Johannes Brandstetter

    Gyrokinetic simulations model the plasma turbulence governing heat transport in magnetically confined fusion devices. These 5D simulations are computationally expensive and produce massive data volumes, with a single snapshot requiring tens of gigabytes of storage. This makes directly storing intermediate timesteps impractical and motivates the use of (lossy) compression. Recent neural compression approaches achieve favorable rate–distortion trade-offs by augmenting conventional $L_2$ reconstruction objectives with physics-informed losses that preserve derived quantities such as the electrostatic potential and heat flux. However, neural network based representations can be difficult to optimize and refine when additional constraints are imposed. We introduce GyroSplat, a compression method for gyrokinetic fields inspired by Gaussian splatting. GyroSplat represents each plasma field as a weighted sum of independent Gaussian–Gabor atoms, yielding a representation that is linear in its coefficients. This linearity enables a staged optimization strategy in which atoms are first fitted to minimize reconstruction error, then refined against the potential, and subsequently new atoms are added to correct the transport. Moreover, relevant derived quantities admit closed-form expressions in terms of the atom coefficients, enabling efficient refinement via a Gauss–Newton procedure. Experiments on gyrokinetic simulation data show that GyroSplat achieves improved trade-offs at matched storage over established compression baselines on derived physical quantities while remaining competitive on field reconstruction, and improving over state-of-the-art physics-informed compressors. These results demonstrate Gaussian splatting as an effective and flexible approach to high-fidelity compression of scientific simulation data.

  • Anatomy of Rollout Error in Chaotic Flow Surrogates

    Emma Gauillard, Armand Kassaï Koupaï, Etienne Meunier, Patrick Gallinari

    Autoregressive neural surrogates for turbulent PDEs are typically evaluated by rollout RMSE against a reference trajectory. However, in chaotic flows, trajectories often decorrelate due to sensitivity to initial conditions, making pointwise predic- tion errors meaningless. We investigate how surrogate errors develop and what aspects of the learned dynamics can still be evaluated beyond this predictability horizon. We compare deterministic and generative surrogates on 2D Kolmogorov flow using a shared backbone, focusing on models whose rollouts remain bounded. Our analysis reveals three findings. First, errors emerge at fine spatial scales before large-scale trajectory decorrelation. Second, despite trajectory divergence, local one-step errors measured against a numerical solver on model-generated states remain approximately constant with rollout depth. Third, one-step prediction ac- curacy does not necessarily translate into accurate long-term state statistics. This highlights the need to complement trajectory-based evaluation with measures of local dynamical accuracy and long-term statistical fidelity.

  • Task-Agnostic Self-Supervised Learning for Physical Dynamics

    Biel Castaño Segade, Joceran Gouneau, Armand Kassaï Koupaï, Lise Le Boudec, Patrick Gallinari

    Physics foundation models are commonly pretrained by forecasting future states, tying representation learning to a specific downstream task. We investigate whether self-supervised learning from partial observations can instead produce task-agnostic representations that capture the hidden dynamics of physical systems. Using a shared ViT backbone for heterogeneous 2D and 3D systems, we study masked reconstruction in physical space and JEPA-style prediction in latent space. To assess what these representations encode about the underlying dynamics, we freeze the encoder and measure how well governing physical parameters can be recovered from its features. To explicitly target properties of the dynamical system that persist across an entire trajectory, we introduce \emph{regime fingerprinting}, which exploits the fact that an early partial view and a broader view of the same trajectory are generated under the same physical regime, and trains their representations to remain identifiable across time. Combined with latent-space prediction, regime fingerprinting yields the strongest recovery of governing parameters in our experiments and compares favorably with forecasting-pretrained baselines. These results suggest that self-supervised learning can capture trajectory-level physical dynamics without using forecasting as a pretraining objective.

  • Grid, Set, or Graph? Representations for Learned VLBI Reconstruction Under Distribution Shift

    Dmitrii Zagorulia

    Radio interferometers measure complex visibilities at irregularly sampled spatial frequencies, with sampling patterns that vary between observations. We investigate how the representation of these measurements affects learned image reconstruction by comparing three approaches: a regular grid processed by a convolutional neural network (CNN), an unordered set processed by DeepSets, and a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph processed by a graph neural network (GNN). The models are trained to reproduce CLEAN images from Astrogeo X-band observations and evaluated without adaptation on the MOJAVE 15 GHz survey. The GNN achieves the lowest median normalized mean squared error (NMSE) on both held-out X-band observations (0.202, compared with 0.228 for DeepSets and 0.376 for the CNN) and MOJAVE (0.386, compared with 0.448 and 0.707). However, all three models exhibit similar relative increases in NMSE under the survey shift (88–96\%), providing no clear evidence of differences in relative robustness. An oracle-scaled mean-image baseline outperforms all three models, while diagnostics on selected observations suggest that amplitude underprediction contributes substantially to the degradation on MOJAVE. Because the survey shift simultaneously changes observing frequency, array configuration, and source characteristics, these results do not isolate the effects of sampling geometry.
